warmup.q: A group of three consumers reads a 6-partition topic with Kafka 4.4's default consumer settings. A fourth consumer starts. While the group rebalances, how many of the six partitions stop being processed?
options: Only the one or two partitions that move to the new consumer
All six: by default every member hands back every partition before the new assignment arrives
None: rebalancing happens in a background thread
Only the partitions of the busiest consumer
warmup.why: The client defaults to the classic protocol, and the default partition.assignment.strategy list, [RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor], uses Range, an eager assignor. Under eager rebalancing every member revokes all of its partitions before it rejoins, so the whole group stops. The first option describes what cooperative rebalancing and the new protocol (group.protocol=consumer) do. You have to choose them.

sections.h: A group divides the partitions, one owner each
sections.html:
Lesson 7 built one consumer: its poll loop, its position and its committed offset. One is rarely enough. One ledger consumer applies about 8 payments a second: each one waits 120 ms for the card issuer. At the end of the month the payments topic receives 30 a second. A single consumer falls 22 payments further behind every second, which is 79,200 after an hour. You need four of them.

The simplest idea is to start four copies of the service. If each copy reads the whole topic, as lesson 2 showed every reader can, then every payment is applied four times. The next idea is to share the records the way lesson 1's queue does: competing consumers, and whoever is free takes the next message. That breaks two things you rely on. Lesson 5 put all of acct-7's records in one partition, in order, so its capture never overtakes its authorization; with two consumers on one partition, the capture can be applied first. And lesson 7's bookmark is one number per partition, which only works if one reader moves it.

Kafka shares the work by partition instead. A consumer group is a set of consumers with the same group.id. The group gives each partition to exactly one member, and a member can own several. With six partitions and three members, each member owns two. Inside a partition, one reader keeps the order. And each partition still has one committed offset for the group.

You've met this design before. The Partitioning track's lesson on rebalancing called it fixed partitions: hash keys into P partitions once, keep a table from partition to owner, and move whole partitions when owners come and go. Kafka uses it twice. Brokers own partitions for storage, and moving one to a new broker means copying its data. Members of a group own partitions for processing, and moving one copies nothing: the records stay on the brokers, and only the owner and the bookmark change hands. The table also gives fan-out for free. A second group, such as fraud-check, keeps its own table and its own bookmarks over the same partitions (figure).

Two consequences follow. Parallelism stops at the partition count: a seventh member of a group on six partitions gets nothing and sits idle. And moving work around means moving partitions, which the rest of this lesson is about.

Who decides who owns what? One broker is the group's coordinator: the broker that leads the partition of __consumer_offsets where the group's commits live. Members tell it they are alive. An assignor turns "these members, these partitions" into a map from partition to member, the assignment. There are three classic recipes. Range hands each member a block of consecutive partitions, topic by topic. Round robin deals all partitions out like cards. Sticky balances the group and moves as few partitions as possible, which is the Partitioning track's test of a good rebalancing scheme: when a member joins, move only its fair share, about 1/(N+1) of the partitions, and only to it. They differ more than you might expect: with two topics of three partitions and two members, range gives one member four partitions and the other two, and round robin gives both three. The lab builds all three.

To join a group, set group.id and call subscribe instead of assign:

Java
var config = Map.<String, Object>of(
        "bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092",
        "group.id", "ledger",                 // the group: members share its partitions
        "group.protocol", "consumer",         // the new rebalance protocol (section 3)
        "enable.auto.commit", false,
        "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class,
        "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class);
var consumer = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(config);
consumer.subscribe(List.of("payments"));      // the group decides which partitions this member reads
Kotlin
val config = mapOf<String, Any>(
    "bootstrap.servers" to "localhost:9092",
    "group.id" to "ledger",                   // the group: members share its partitions
    "group.protocol" to "consumer",           // the new rebalance protocol (section 3)
    "enable.auto.commit" to false,
    "key.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
    "value.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
)
val consumer = KafkaConsumer<String, String>(config)
consumer.subscribe(listOf("payments"))        // the group decides which partitions this member reads

try.title: Watch three consumers split six partitions
steps: From the labs folder, start the broker: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait.

Run GroupDemo (command below). It writes 10 payments to each partition of the 6-partition topic ledger-rebalance, then starts three consumers of one new group, one after the other, on the new protocol. Each one prints what the group gives it and takes away. Before a partition leaves, its listener commits how far it got.
Predict before you run it: when c3 joins, which partitions does it get, and does c1 stop processing the ones it keeps?

Describe the group it used (the name is on the first line): docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group <name>.

Each prints what * the group gives it and takes away. Before a partition leaves, its listener commits how far it got: the handover. * Arguments: "consumer" (the new protocol, the default), "cooperative" (classic, CooperativeStickyAssignor) * or "eager" (classic, RangeAssignor); then "nohandover" to skip the commit when a partition leaves. */ public class GroupDemo { static long start = System.nanoTime(); static final Map<String, Set<Integer>> owned = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // what each member owns now static final Map<String, Integer> revoked = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // partitions each member handed back static final AtomicBoolean stop = new AtomicBoolean(false); static boolean handover = true; static final AtomicLong processed = new AtomicLong(); // records processed by the group static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5.1fs %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e9, msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "consumer"; handover = !(args.length > 1 && args[1].equals("nohandover")); String topic = "ledger-rebalance"; try (var admin = Admin.create(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092"))) { if (!admin.listTopics().names().get().contains(topic)) admin.createTopics(List.of(new NewTopic(topic, 6, (short) 1))).all().get(); } try (var p = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class))) { for (int part = 0; part < 6; part++) for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) p.send(new ProducerRecord<>(topic, part, "acct-" + part, "pay-" + i)); } long total; // every record so far try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) { List<TopicPartition> tps = new ArrayList<>(); for (int part = 0; part < 6; part++) tps.add(new TopicPartition(topic, part)); total = c.endOffsets(tps).values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); } Map<String, Object> config = new HashMap<>(Map.of( "bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "group.id", "ledger-" + mode + "-" + System.currentTimeMillis(), // a new group every run "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "enable.auto.commit", false, "auto.offset.reset", "earliest")); switch (mode) { case "eager" -> config.put("partition.assignment.strategy", RangeAssignor.class.getName()); case "cooperative" -> config.put("partition.assignment.strategy", CooperativeStickyAssignor.class.getName()); default -> config.put("group.protocol", "consumer"); } System.out.println("mode " + mode + ", group " + config.get("group.id") + (handover ? "" : ", no handover commits")); List<Thread> members = new ArrayList<>(); start = System.nanoTime(); // the clock starts when c1 joins for (String name : List.of("c1", "c2", "c3")) { log(name + " joins"); Map<String, Object> memberConfig = new HashMap<>(config); memberConfig.put("client.id", name); Thread t = new Thread(() -> runMember(name, memberConfig, topic)); t.start(); members.add(t); int n = members.size(); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + 30_000_000_000L; // wait until the group is balanced again, and has read every record while (!(owned.size() == n && owned.values().stream().allMatch(s -> s.size() == 6 / n) && processed.get() >= total) && System.nanoTime() < deadline) Thread.sleep(50); } Thread.sleep(1_000); // let the last heartbeats settle before everyone leaves stop.set(true); for (Thread t : members) t.join(); System.out.println("partitions handed back: " + revoked + ", " + revoked.values().stream().mapToInt(i -> i).sum() + " in all"); System.out.println("records processed: " + processed.get() + ", records in the topic: " + total); } static void runMember(String name, Map<String, Object> config, String topic) { try { memberLoop(name, config, topic); } catch (KafkaException e) { if (!stop.get()) throw e; // closing while the group still moves partitions is harmless at the end of a demo } } static void memberLoop(String name, Map<String, Object> config, String topic) { try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(config)) { c.subscribe(List.of(topic), new ConsumerRebalanceListener() { @Override public void onPartitionsRevoked(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) { if (partitions.isEmpty()) return; // the loop below processes every record it polls, so the position is how far this member got Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> offsets = new HashMap<>(); for (TopicPartition tp : partitions) offsets.put(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(c.position(tp))); if (handover) c.commitSync(offsets); if (!stop.get()) { // closing at the end: commit, but stay quiet revoked.merge(name, partitions.size(), Integer::sum); log(name + " revoked " + numbers(partitions) + (handover ? ", committed " + positions(c, partitions) : ", committed nothing")); } Set<Integer> left = new TreeSet<>(owned.getOrDefault(name, Set.of())); left.removeAll(numbers(partitions)); owned.put(name, left); } @Override public void onPartitionsAssigned(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) { Set<Integer> now = numbers(c.assignment()); if (!partitions.isEmpty()) // the positions start at the committed offsets log(name + " assigned " + numbers(partitions) + ", starts at " + positions(c, partitions) + ", owns " + now); owned.put(name, now); } }); while (!stop.get()) processed.addAndGet(c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(100)).count()); // "processing" is free here } } static Set<Integer> numbers(Collection<TopicPartition> tps) { return tps.stream().map(TopicPartition::partition).collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new)); } static List<Long> positions(KafkaConsumer<String, String> c, Collection<TopicPartition> tps) { return tps.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(TopicPartition::partition)).map(c::position).toList(); } }

sections.h: Moving a partition means handing over its bookmark
sections.html:
Whenever a member joins or leaves, partitions change owner. That is a rebalance. The partition moves, but what about its bookmark?

Take partition 3. c1 owns it and has processed up to offset 341. It commits after every batch of 100, so the group's committed offset is 300. Now the group gives partition 3 to c2. c2 starts where the group's bookmark says, at 300, and processes 300 to 340 a second time. With the default max.poll.records of 500, one rebalance can replay up to a whole batch. And if c1 is still working through its batch when c2 starts, both apply the same payments at the same moment.

The fix is to tell c1 before the partition leaves. You register a ConsumerRebalanceListener with subscribe(topics, listener), and the consumer calls it from inside poll, on your polling thread:

  • onPartitionsRevoked(partitions): these partitions are leaving, and they are still yours. Finish or abandon the current work on them and commit how far you got. This is the handover.
  • onPartitionsAssigned(partitions): these are new. The consumer will start at their committed offsets. If you keep offsets in your own database, seek here instead.
  • onPartitionsLost(partitions): the group already gave these to someone else, usually because this member was thrown out (section 4). Don't commit: the new owner's bookmark is no longer yours to move.
Java
consumer.subscribe(List.of("payments"), new ConsumerRebalanceListener() {
    public void onPartitionsRevoked(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) {
        consumer.commitSync(processedOffsets(partitions));   // the next owner starts exactly here
    }
    public void onPartitionsAssigned(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) { }
    public void onPartitionsLost(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) {
        forget(partitions);                                  // not ours any more: no commit
    }
});
Kotlin
consumer.subscribe(listOf("payments"), object : ConsumerRebalanceListener {
    override fun onPartitionsRevoked(partitions: Collection<TopicPartition>) {
        consumer.commitSync(processedOffsets(partitions))    // the next owner starts exactly here
    }
    override fun onPartitionsAssigned(partitions: Collection<TopicPartition>) {}
    override fun onPartitionsLost(partitions: Collection<TopicPartition>) {
        forget(partitions)                                   // not ours any more: no commit
    }
})

processedOffsets is yours to write: the next offset to read of each partition, counting only records that are fully processed. That is lesson 7's rule, last processed plus one. If the loop processes everything it polls before it polls again, consumer.position(tp) is that number.

The handover is safe because of an ordering rule. The group never gives a partition to its new owner until the old owner has revoked it. So c1's commit in onPartitionsRevoked always lands before c2 reads the committed offset. A rebalance can still repeat records, if a member dies without revoking, which is why the ledger from lesson 7 stays idempotent. But a planned rebalance repeats nothing.

sections.h: Eager, cooperative and the new protocol stop different things
sections.html:
How a group rebalances depends on the protocol it speaks, and Kafka 4.4 has two.

The classic protocol works in rounds. When membership changes, the coordinator tells every member to rejoin (a JoinGroup request), waits until all of them have, picks one member as the group leader, and lets that member run the assignor. Then it sends each member its share (SyncGroup). Two flavours run on top of it.

Eager is the original. A member rejoins empty-handed: before JoinGroup it revokes every partition it owns. Nothing is processed until the new assignment arrives, and a group with 100 members waits for the slowest of them. Frames 1 to 3 of the stepper show it. It is also what you get by default: the consumer's default partition.assignment.strategy is [RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor], and the docs say it uses Range, an eager assignor, until you remove Range from the list. By the Partitioning track's test, eager fails twice: it stops every partition, and it can move partitions between old members that didn't need to move.

Cooperative rebalancing (KIP-429, Kafka 2.4) keeps the rounds but lets members keep their partitions while they rejoin. The assignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor, works out which partitions must move. Their owners revoke only those, and a second round assigns them. Nobody else stops, but every move costs two rounds.

The new consumer group protocol (KIP-848, generally available since Kafka 4.0) drops the rounds. Each member sends a heartbeat every few seconds and the coordinator answers. The coordinator runs the assignor itself (uniform by default, or range) whenever membership changes, and keeps a target assignment. Each member compares what it owns with its target and moves toward it on its own: first it revokes what it must give up, then the coordinator assigns it what others have released. There is no group-wide barrier, members that keep their partitions never notice, and there is no leader to wait for. Frames 4 to 6 show it.

You must opt in. The broker side is on by default in 4.0 and later, but the client default for group.protocol is still classic in 4.4. Set group.protocol=consumer. Three classic settings then belong to the broker instead: session.timeout.ms, heartbeat.interval.ms and partition.assignment.strategy all fail with a ConfigException if you set them on the client. The broker's group.consumer.* settings replace them, and group.remote.assignor picks a broker assignor. You can move a group from classic to the new protocol with a rolling restart, one instance at a time; the mixed group keeps working.

The new protocol has one cost: assignments travel on heartbeats, so a member learns about a change only on its next heartbeat, every 5 seconds by default (group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms). The lab broker uses 1 second so the demos finish quickly.

refs.title: KIP-848: The next generation of the consumer rebalance protocol

sections.h: Two clocks decide when a member is gone
sections.html:
A rebalance also starts when the group decides a member is gone. It decides with two separate clocks, and they catch different failures.

The first clock checks that the process is alive. A background thread in the client sends heartbeats. If the coordinator hears nothing for the session timeout, 45 seconds by default, it removes the member and gives its partitions away. That catches a crash, a kill -9 or a pulled network cable, and it means a crashed member's partitions sit unread for up to 45 seconds. A member that closes cleanly with close() leaves at once instead. On the classic protocol the client settings session.timeout.ms and heartbeat.interval.ms (3 s) control this clock; on the new one the broker's group.consumer.session.timeout.ms and group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms do.

The second clock checks that your loop is making progress. Heartbeats keep flowing even while your code is stuck in a card-issuer call, so heartbeats alone can't catch that. If your code doesn't call poll again within max.poll.interval.ms, 5 minutes by default, the client leaves the group by itself. In SlowConsumerDemo c1 has a 4-second limit and one payment takes 8 seconds. At 4 seconds c1 leaves, and a second later c2 owns c1's partition and processes it from the last commit. When c1 comes back, it finishes the records it was holding, so they are processed twice. Its commit fails with CommitFailedException, and its next poll reports the partitions as lost and rejoins. Lesson 7 gave the fix: lower max.poll.records until a batch fits easily inside the limit.

Watch for the loop this can start. A member that is slow because its partitions are busy gets thrown out. Its partitions land on the others, which are now busier and slower, so they overrun the limit too, and the group rebalances again and again while lag climbs. It is the cascading failure the Partitioning track warned about, an overloaded node declared dead and its load moved onto the rest, and the Faults track's lesson on timeouts explains why a slow member and a dead one look alike from outside. The fix is the same as there: set the limit with a margin over the slowest normal batch, not the average one.

Deploys are the third source of rebalances. A rolling restart of six instances means six leaves and six joins: twelve rebalances in a few minutes, with each partition moving to another member and back. Static membership stops that. Give each instance a stable group.instance.id, such as ledger-3 for pod 3 of a StatefulSet. A static member that shuts down keeps its partitions, nobody else is disturbed, and when an instance with the same id comes back within the session timeout it gets the same partitions. The price is that if it doesn't come back, its partitions wait the full session timeout before anyone takes them.

How do you see a group falling behind? With lag, from lesson 2: for each partition, the log end offset minus the group's committed offset. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe prints it per partition. Lag that grows steadily means too few consumers or slow processing. Lag that jumps on every partition at once, again and again, usually means the group keeps rebalancing.

refs.title: Kafka 4.4 consumer configs: max.poll.interval.ms, group.instance.id, group.protocol

analogy: A consumer group is a team of cashiers and the partitions are checkout lanes. Each lane has one cashier at a time, so the customers in a lane are served in order, and each lane keeps its own tally sheet of how far it got. When a cashier arrives or goes home, the supervisor reassigns lanes. The old way (eager) is to close every lane, collect every tally sheet and hand out a new plan of who works which lane. The new way is to tap only the cashiers whose lanes move: they finish the customer in front of them, hand over the tally sheet, and the new cashier carries on from the last tick. The analogy breaks at the tally sheet: a real cashier can't forget to hand it over, but a Kafka consumer that commits nothing on revoke silently makes the next one serve the same customers again.
world: Your Quarkus payment services join groups through the SmallRye Kafka connector, so check what it passes to the client: on kafka-clients 4.x you can set group.protocol=consumer as an ordinary consumer property on the channel, and you then have to remove session.timeout.ms and heartbeat.interval.ms, which the client rejects with that protocol. Each pod of a Kubernetes StatefulSet has a stable name, which makes it a natural group.instance.id, so rolling deploys stop shuffling partitions. If a payment needs a slow call, such as a fraud check or an issuer that can take seconds, size max.poll.records so a full batch takes well under max.poll.interval.ms. If the work belongs in a Temporal workflow, start the workflow from the consumer and keep the poll loop fast. And alert on lag per partition, not just per group: one stuck partition hides inside a healthy average.
mistake: Leaving the defaults and assuming rebalances are cheap. The default classic assignor is eager, so every deploy, scale-up or slow batch stops the whole group, and teams see it only as lag spikes with no errors. It gets worse when processing is slow: a batch that overruns max.poll.interval.ms gets the member thrown out, which triggers a rebalance, which delays everyone's next poll, and the group rebalances in a loop. The fix: set group.protocol=consumer (or at least CooperativeStickyAssignor), commit in onPartitionsRevoked, keep batches well inside max.poll.interval.ms with a smaller max.poll.records, and use group.instance.id for instances that restart often.

compare.title: A rebalance listener that hands the bookmark over, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: class Handover implements ConsumerRebalanceListener { private final Consumer<String, String> consumer; private final Map<TopicPartition, Long> done = new HashMap<>(); // next offset to read, per partition Handover(Consumer<String, String> consumer) { this.consumer = consumer; } void processed(ConsumerRecord<String, String> r) { done.put(new TopicPartition(r.topic(), r.partition()), r.offset() + 1); } @Override public void onPartitionsRevoked(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) { Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> offsets = new HashMap<>(); for (TopicPartition tp : partitions) { Long next = done.remove(tp); if (next != null) offsets.put(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(next)); } if (!offsets.isEmpty()) consumer.commitSync(offsets); } @Override public void onPartitionsAssigned(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) { } @Override public void onPartitionsLost(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) { partitions.forEach(done::remove); // never commit a lost partition } }

compare.note: The same three callbacks. Java has to override onPartitionsLost to stop the interface's default, which simply calls onPartitionsRevoked and would commit a partition that is no longer yours; Kotlin's override does the same job. Kotlin builds the offsets map in one expression with mapNotNull and toMap, where Java fills a HashMap in a loop. Both keep done as a plain map, without locks: the consumer calls the listener on the polling thread, inside poll, so nothing else touches it at the same time.

recap: A consumer group shares a topic by partition: each partition has exactly one owner in the group and one committed offset per group. Members beyond the partition count sit idle.
A rebalance moves partitions when members join or leave. Commit in onPartitionsRevoked so the next owner starts exactly where you stopped; never commit in onPartitionsLost.
The default classic assignor list uses Range, an eager assignor: every member hands back everything on every rebalance. Cooperative rebalancing moves only what must move, in two rounds.
The new protocol (KIP-848, group.protocol=consumer) lets the broker compute assignments and each member reconcile on its own: revoke first, then assign. The 4.4 client still defaults to classic.
Heartbeats and the session timeout (45 s) catch dead processes; max.poll.interval.ms (5 min) catches stuck loops. Static membership (group.instance.id) keeps partitions through a restart.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why every deploy of the ledger service causes a lag spike on all partitions and a few duplicate payments in the logs. Explain what happens during the deploy and what you would change.
explain.answer: Each pod that stops leaves the group and each pod that starts joins it, so a rolling deploy causes one rebalance per step. We run the classic protocol with the default assignor, which is eager: on every rebalance every member hands back all of its partitions and waits for the new assignment, so all partitions stop at once. That is the lag spike. The duplicates come from the handover: our consumer commits after each batch but not in onPartitionsRevoked, so a partition that moves restarts at the last batch commit and the new owner reapplies what the old owner had already done; the idempotency check catches them, which is why we only see them in logs. I would switch to group.protocol=consumer so only the partitions that move pause, add a rebalance listener that commits processed offsets on revoke and commits nothing on lost, and give each pod a group.instance.id from its StatefulSet name, so a restarting pod keeps its partitions and nothing moves at all.

deeper.html:
Epochs keep the new protocol honest. KIP-848 tracks three counters. The group epoch goes up whenever membership or subscriptions change. The target assignment carries the epoch it was computed for. Each member has a member epoch, and it advances only once that member has reconciled to the target. A heartbeat or commit from a member with an old epoch is refused with FENCED_MEMBER_EPOCH, which is how the coordinator stops a member that missed a change from acting on stale partitions.

Regex subscriptions moved to the broker. With the new protocol, subscribe(SubscriptionPattern) sends an RE2/J pattern to the coordinator, which resolves it against the cluster's topics. A new topic that matches is picked up without every client polling metadata. Only the new protocol supports it.

Range still matters for joins. If two topics are partitioned the same way (say payments and refunds, both keyed by account and both with 12 partitions), Range gives partition 3 of both to the same member, so a consumer can join them locally. The broker's range assignor keeps that property; set group.remote.assignor=range to get it. The lab's test that one member gets the extra partition of every topic is that property seen from the other side.

Share groups are a different tool. Lesson 11 covers share groups, where several members read the same partition and each record is acknowledged on its own. They give up per-partition order to get more consumers than partitions.
